candidate_concepts.label: Real Options Augment DCF Valuation
candidate_concepts.description: Real option pricing serves as an augmentation to discounted cash flow valuation by capturing the value of managerial flexibility (options to delay, expand, abandon) that traditional DCF underestimates.
coverage_criteria: Explain why traditional DCF can undervalue assets with embedded flexibility.
Identify at least two types of real options (delay, expand, abandon).

extraction_reason.source_grounded_rationale: The source explicitly states that option pricing is not an alternative to DCF but an augmentation, and lists three option types that DCF misses.
extraction_reason.granularity_rationale: This is a foundational concept that students must grasp before applying option pricing. It is small enough to be checked with a few explanatory questions.

candidate_concepts.label: Learning and Adaptive Behavior as Source of Option Value
candidate_concepts.description: Real option value stems from the opportunity to observe outcomes (learn) and adjust actions accordingly (adaptive behavior), transforming a seemingly negative expected value investment into a positive one when staged.
coverage_criteria: Restate why a two-step investment can have a higher expected value than a one-step investment with the same overall probabilities.
Define 'learning' and 'adaptive behavior' in the context of real options.

extraction_reason.source_grounded_rationale: The video explicitly breaks down a bad investment into two steps and attributes the increased value to learning and adaptive behavior, calling them the 'two key words'.
extraction_reason.granularity_rationale: This core intuition separates real options from simple DCF; it is a self-contained teachable idea checkable via a simple example.

candidate_concepts.label: Using Payoff Diagrams to Identify Real Options
candidate_concepts.description: A real option exists when the payoff structure of a decision resembles a call or put option payoff diagram, featuring a kinked payoff that limits downside losses while allowing upside gains.
coverage_criteria: Sketch a call option payoff diagram and label the strike price.
Explain how limited losses and potential unlimited gains create option value.

extraction_reason.source_grounded_rationale: The source demonstrates how to recognize an option by drawing payoff diagrams for calls and puts and states that if the payoff looks like an option diagram, you have an option.
extraction_reason.granularity_rationale: This is a specific, visual criterion that students can apply directly; checking it requires them to draw and explain the diagram, which is a focused task.

candidate_concepts.label: Three Definitional Characteristics of a Real Option
candidate_concepts.description: For an asset or decision to contain a real option, it must have: (1) a clearly defined underlying asset whose value changes unpredictably, (2) contingent payoffs triggered by a specific event, and (3) a limited life.
coverage_criteria: List the three characteristics.
For a given business scenario, identify whether these characteristics are present.

extraction_reason.source_grounded_rationale: The video explicitly states three specific characteristics: derivative securities with underlying asset, contingent payoffs, limited lives.
extraction_reason.granularity_rationale: This is a precise checklist that can be taught and tested in three simple questions.

candidate_concepts.label: Exclusivity as the Driver of Significant Option Value
candidate_concepts.description: An option only has significant economic value if there is exclusivity—the holder alone can exercise it. Without exclusivity (e.g., anyone can buy at market price), the option value is zero.
coverage_criteria: Explain why exclusivity is necessary for a real option to have economic value.
Contrast the landlord anecdote scenario with a proprietary technology option.

extraction_reason.source_grounded_rationale: The video emphasizes exclusivity as the key word, using the MBA student anecdote to show that without exclusivity the option is worthless.
extraction_reason.granularity_rationale: This is a critical filter that students must apply; it is a single clear concept with a memorable example, making it checkable.

candidate_concepts.label: Six Determinants of Real Option Value
candidate_concepts.description: The value of a real option is influenced by six factors: underlying asset value, variance of that value, expected dividends, strike price, option life, and interest rates, with variance uniquely increasing option value.
coverage_criteria: List the six determinants.
Explain why higher variance increases option value, contrary to DCF.
Predict the effect of higher interest rates on a call option.

extraction_reason.source_grounded_rationale: The video enumerates exactly six determinants, dividing them into those relating to the underlying asset, the option, and interest rates, and stresses the counterintuitive role of variance.
extraction_reason.granularity_rationale: These six factors form a compact set that can be memorized and applied; checking requires recall and simple application.

candidate_concepts.label: Replication and Arbitrage Principles in Option Pricing
candidate_concepts.description: Option pricing models rely on two principles: (1) replication—constructing a portfolio of the underlying asset and borrowing/lending that mimics the option's payoffs; (2) arbitrage—if two assets have identical payoffs, they must have the same price.
coverage_criteria: Describe what a replicating portfolio is.
Explain why arbitrage forces options and replicating portfolios to have equal prices.

extraction_reason.source_grounded_rationale: The video clearly states that all option pricing models are built on replication and arbitrage, defining each.
extraction_reason.granularity_rationale: These are two fundamental financial concepts that underpin the models; they can be checked with simple definitions and reasoning.

candidate_concepts.label: Trade-offs Between Black-Scholes and Binomial Models for Real Options
candidate_concepts.description: The Black-Scholes model assumes European exercise, constant variance, and no jumps, requiring only six inputs. The binomial model allows early exercise and changing variances but demands detailed price path data, often infeasible for real assets.
coverage_criteria: State the key restrictive assumptions of Black-Scholes.
Contrast the data requirements of the binomial model with its flexibility.
Articulate why practitioners might still prefer Black-Scholes despite its limitations.

extraction_reason.source_grounded_rationale: The video compares both models explicitly, highlighting Black-Scholes' parsimony versus binomial's generality but data demands.
extraction_reason.granularity_rationale: This is a practical decision point for practitioners; the comparison can be tested by asking students to list pros/cons.

candidate_concepts.label: Three Tests for Applying Real Option Valuation
candidate_concepts.description: To validly apply real option valuation, three tests must be passed: (1) identify an embedded option, (2) verify exclusivity, (3) ensure the underlying asset and option are tradeable enough for option pricing models to work.
coverage_criteria: List the three tests.
For a given case, argue whether a test is satisfied.

extraction_reason.source_grounded_rationale: The video concludes by summarizing these three tests as essential filters before using option pricing.
extraction_reason.granularity_rationale: This is a high-level checklist that integrates the session; it is checkable by having students recall and apply the tests.
